1.title: Privacy Laws Applied to AI
1.text: Welcome to Module four: Privacy Laws Applied to A I. This opens domain two, which is about laws, standards and frameworks. Competency A asks how existing data privacy laws apply to A I. We will use the G D P R as the main example, with US state laws alongside, and we follow Helios through a privacy request.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do four things. Explain how notice, choice, the lawful basis and the limits on purpose apply to A I. Explain data minimization and privacy by design for A I. Explain the controller's duties: assessments, processors, transfers, rights, automated decisions, breaches and records. And explain the rules for sensitive and special-category data, including biometrics.

1.title: Case Check-In: An Applicant Asks What Helios Holds
1.text: At Helios, an applicant in the European Union writes to ask what Helios holds about them, and how the hiring tool scored them. The tool also analyzes a video interview, and Veridex hosts the data in the United States. Jonas Weber, Head of Legal and Privacy, must answer within the legal deadline. Over this module you will see which privacy duties are in play, and who carries them.

1.title: Why Privacy Law Reaches AI
1.text: This is a beyond-the-Body-of-Knowledge slide. Personal data is any information relating to an identified or identifiable person, in Article four, point one of the G D P R, the General Data Protection Regulation. Processing is any operation on it. In an A I system, personal data appears in training data, in inputs and prompts, in outputs, and in inferences about people. Profiling is automated evaluation of personal aspects. The controller decides purposes and means, and the processor acts on its behalf. U S state laws, such as Colorado's, use the same ideas. Exam tip: if data relate to an identifiable person at any stage, privacy law applies.

1.title: Transparency and Notice for AI
1.text: This is a beyond-the-Body-of-Knowledge slide. The G D P R requires processing that is lawful, fair and transparent, in Article five. Information must be concise, intelligible, easy to find, and in clear and plain language, Article twelve. It is given at collection under Article thirteen, or within the set time when data come from elsewhere, under Article fourteen. For A I, the notice must mention automated decision-making, including profiling, and meaningful information about the logic involved. Say that A I is used, for what, and with what effect. Exam tip: transparency about A I is part of privacy notice.

1.title: Choice, Consent and the Lawful Basis
1.text: This is a beyond-the-Body-of-Knowledge slide, tagged verify live. Article six lists six lawful bases: consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public task, and legitimate interests. Consent must be freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous, and it is weak where there is a power imbalance, as in employment. No basis is ranked above another. Legitimate interests need a three-step test: a real interest, necessity, and balancing against people's rights, as the European Data Protection Board, or E D P B, explained in its Opinion twenty-eight of twenty twenty-four. As of the twenty-seventh of October, twenty twenty-six, proposed G D P R changes for A I training, a new Article eighty-eight C, were not confirmed as adopted. Exam tip: consent is not always the basis.

1.title: Purpose Limitation and Reuse of Data
1.text: Purpose limitation says data must be collected for specified, explicit and legitimate purposes, and not used in an incompatible way. That is Article five, paragraph one, point b. To judge compatibility, weigh five factors from Article six, paragraph four: the link between the purposes, the context, the nature of the data, the consequences for people, and the safeguards. If the new purpose is not compatible, it needs its own basis, such as consent, or it should not proceed. At Helios, application data are not automatically fit to train a screening model. Exam tip: for reuse, ask whether the new purpose is compatible.

1.title: What the Exam Asks: Notice, Choice, Basis, Purpose
1.text: Here are the usual traps. Notice must be specific to the use: it names A I, the purpose and the effect. Consent is one basis of six, and often the wrong one in employment. A basis is needed for each purpose, including training and reuse. Purpose limitation blocks silent reuse. Legitimate interests is not a default; it needs a balancing test. And penalties: breaches of principles, lawful basis and rights can be fined up to twenty million euros or four percent of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher, under Article eighty-three. Exam tip: establish the basis before using the data.

1.title: Data Minimization in AI Systems
1.text: Data must be adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary for the purposes. That is Article five, paragraph one, point c. Data must also be accurate and kept no longer than necessary. For A I, that means choosing features for the purpose, dropping what the model does not need, and setting retention limits for training sets. The E D P B asks, for legitimate-interest training, whether there is a less intrusive way and whether the amount of data is proportionate. More data for a better model is not a legal defense. Exam tip: the least data that does the job.

1.title: Privacy by Design and by Default
1.text: This is a beyond-the-Body-of-Knowledge slide. Article twenty-five has two parts. By design: build measures, such as pseudonymization, into the system from the start. By default: process only the data needed for each purpose, in the amount, extent, storage period and accessibility. Privacy-enhancing techniques help. Pseudonymization replaces identifiers, with extra information kept apart. Differential privacy adds noise so no single person can be singled out. Federated learning trains where the data live and shares model updates, not data. Synthetic data mimic patterns of real data. Exam tip: privacy by default means the narrowest setting at the start.

1.title: The Tension: Data-Hungry Models and Minimization
1.text: Here is the tension. Model teams want more data, kept longer, from more sources. The law asks for the necessary amount, for the purpose, for as long as needed. Governance resolves it with a defined purpose, curated data, privacy-enhancing techniques and retention limits. And it documents the necessity reasoning, because regulators ask for it. Exam tip: the answer is neither more data nor no A I. It is purpose, curation and technique, with a record.

1.title: Controller, Processor and Joint Controller in AI
1.text: This is a beyond-the-Body-of-Knowledge slide. The controller decides purposes and means. The processor acts on documented instructions. Joint controllers decide together and must set out who does what, and people may exercise rights against each, under Article twenty-six. At Helios, Helios is the controller of applicant data. Veridex screens on its instructions, so it is a processor. But if Veridex uses the data to improve its own model, it decides a purpose of its own, and may become a controller or joint controller. Corvid Labs is a processor for chats sent through its interface, on the same test. Exam tip: the label follows who decides.

2.title: Impact Assessments: DPIA and Its Relatives
2.text: This is a beyond-the-Body-of-Knowledge slide. A data protection impact assessment is required before processing that is likely to result in a high risk to people. That is Article thirty-five, paragraph one. Named cases include systematic, extensive evaluation based on automated processing, such as profiling, and large-scale special-category data. The minimum content is a description and purposes, necessity and proportionality, risks, and measures. Seek the data protection officer's advice. In the U S, Colorado requires a documented assessment for profiling with defined risks and for sensitive data. A D P I A feeds the A I impact assessments of modules eight and twelve. Exam tip: a scoring hiring tool is a textbook case.

2.title: Third-Party Processors and Sub-Processors
2.text: Article twenty-eight governs processors. The controller must use processors with sufficient guarantees. A binding contract requires processing only on documented instructions, confidentiality, security, help with rights and assessments, deletion or return of data, and audit information. Sub-processors need the controller's written authorization, they carry the same duties, and the first processor stays fully liable. In A I supply chains, a model provider or cloud host is often a sub-processor. Ask for the list, and bar use of your data to train the vendor's own models. Exam tip: a processor contract is mandatory.

2.title: Cross-Border Transfers
2.text: This is a beyond-the-Body-of-Knowledge slide, tagged verify live. Chapter five of the G D P R governs transfers, in Articles forty-four to forty-nine. First, an adequacy decision under Article forty-five: the Commission finds a country, territory or sector adequate. Otherwise, appropriate safeguards under Article forty-six: standard data protection clauses, binding corporate rules, an approved code of conduct or certification. A I cases include training or inference in another region, a hosted model interface abroad, and remote support access. As of the twenty-seventh of October, twenty twenty-six, adequacy decisions, such as the E U-U S Data Privacy Framework, can be challenged. Exam tip: remote access is a transfer too.

2.title: Data Subject Rights Applied to AI
2.text: This is a beyond-the-Body-of-Knowledge slide. Five rights matter most. Access, Article fifteen: a copy of the data, and for automated decisions, meaningful information about the logic involved. Rectification, Article sixteen: fix wrong data. Erasure, Article seventeen, with grounds such as data no longer needed or withdrawn consent. Portability, Article twenty, for data the person provided under consent or contract. Objection, Article twenty-one, to processing based on public task or legitimate interests. Answer within one month, extendable by two months. Erasure from a trained model is hard, so keep personal data out of training where possible. Exam tip: match the right to the request.

2.title: Automated Decision-Making: Article 22 and the SCHUFA Ruling
2.text: This is a beyond-the-Body-of-Knowledge slide, tagged dates. Article twenty-two, paragraph one, gives a right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing, including profiling, with legal or similarly significant effects. Exceptions: a contract, authorization by law with safeguards, or explicit consent. Safeguards: at least human intervention, the chance to express a view, and to contest the decision. Special-category data only with explicit consent or substantial public interest. On the seventh of December, twenty twenty-three, the Court of Justice ruled in SCHUFA that an automated credit score can itself be a decision, where a third party draws strongly on it. Exam tip: a rubber-stamp review does not make it human.

2.title: Incidents, Breach Notification and Records
2.text: A processor tells the controller without undue delay. The controller notifies the authority without undue delay and, where feasible, within seventy-two hours of becoming aware, unless the breach is unlikely to result in a risk. That is Article thirty-three. If the risk is high, inform the people without undue delay, under Article thirty-four, unless the data were protected, for example by encryption. Document every breach. For records, Article thirty requires a record of processing activities, covering purposes, data, recipients, transfers, retention and security. Exam tip: the seventy-two hours run from becoming aware, and a late notice must give its reasons.

2.title: Sensitive and Special-Category Data
2.text: This is a beyond-the-Body-of-Knowledge slide. Article nine lists the special categories: racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religious or philosophical beliefs, trade union membership, genetic data, biometric data for unique identification, data concerning health, and sex life or sexual orientation. Processing is prohibited unless an exception applies, such as explicit consent, employment law obligations, substantial public interest or legal claims. Data that reveal a sensitive characteristic can count even when inferred, and proxies can do the same. U S laws define sensitive data differently. Exam tip: the test is what the data reveal. An inferred health condition is sensitive.

2.title: Biometrics, Children and Other High-Risk Data
2.text: This is a beyond-the-Body-of-Knowledge slide. Biometric data result from technical processing of physical, physiological or behavioral traits and allow or confirm unique identification, in Article four, point fourteen. Used to identify, they are special-category data. The Illinois biometric privacy act requires informed written release before collection, a published retention and destruction policy, and damages of one thousand or five thousand dollars; those details come from secondary sources. For children, where consent is the basis for online services, the age is sixteen, which Member States may lower to thirteen, under Article eight. Module six covers AI-specific rules. Exam tip: biometric data are sensitive when used to identify.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Let us recap. Tell people about A I use, pick and document a lawful basis, and check compatibility before reuse. Use the least data, built in from the start and by default, with privacy-enhancing techniques. As controller: assess with a D P I A, contract processors, secure transfers, answer rights, control automated decisions, notify breaches and keep records. Sensitive data is prohibited unless an exception applies, and what data reveal counts. And controller, processor and joint controller follow who decides purposes and means.

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. Helios wants to use past applicants' data to train a better screening model. The data were collected only to process each application. Under the G D P R, which question should be answered first? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Reusing data for a new purpose needs a compatibility check, or a new lawful basis, and the controller must document it.

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. Which two measures best serve data minimization and privacy by design in a screening model? Select two. The five options are on the screen. The answers are A and C. Minimization limits data to what the purpose needs, and measures such as pseudonymization with access and retention limits support it. Collecting everything, keeping data indefinitely, and publishing the dataset work against it.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. Helios plans to send E U applicants' data to Veridex's servers in the United States. Which statement is correct? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. A transfer to a third country needs an adequacy decision or appropriate safeguards, such as standard data protection clauses, whether the recipient is a controller or a processor.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. An E U job applicant is rejected automatically by a score, with no human review. The applicant asks for a copy of their data, a correction of a wrong employment date, and an explanation of how the score was reached. Which three rights are engaged? Select three. The five options are on the screen. The answers are B, D and E. Access, rectification, and meaningful information about the logic of an automated decision. Nothing asks for erasure or portability.

2.title: Practice Question 5
2.text: Question five. A model infers an applicant's health condition from a video interview and uses it in scoring. How does the G D P R treat the inferred information? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Data that reveal a sensitive characteristic, such as health, fall under the special categories even when inferred, so a prohibition applies unless an Article nine exception is met.

2.title: Answers at a Glance
2.text: Here are all five answers. Question one: B. Question two: A and C. Question three: D. Question four: B, D and E. Question five: C. That completes Module four. Next, Module five covers other existing laws applied to A I: intellectual property, nondiscrimination, consumer protection and product liability.
